title: The nasal dots
hook: two marks, one hum: why does Gurmukhi keep both the tippi and the bindi?
tomorrow: why do some copies have no spaces between the words?

segments.voice: Yesterday, laga matra: the vowel signs that hang on Gurmukhi letters, and one quiet tail at the end of sach doing grammar more than sound. The small signs. There were dots up top, too.
screen: `LAGA MATRA: THE SMALL SIGNS.` → `DOTS UP TOP, TOO.`

segments.voice: One period after ok, and a friend texts back: are you mad? The letters didn't change. A dot did. Gurmukhi has small marks of its own riding above the letters, and they come with a puzzle. Take sangat, the gathering of people around the Guru's words. Over its first letter sits a tiny curved mark: a tippi. Now take maan, the word for mother. The same kind of hum through the nose, but this time the mark is a single dot: a bindi. Two marks, doing what sounds like one job. Why would a script keep both?
screen: `ONE DOT: ARE YOU MAD?` → `SANGAT: A TIPPI.` → `MAAN: A BINDI.` → `TWO MARKS, ONE JOB?`

segments.voice: Here's the answer. The tippi and the bindi both add a nasal sound, the hum of the n in sangat. Which one a word takes depends on its neighbor, the vowel sign on that letter. In the rule learners are taught, a long aa, as in maan, takes the bindi. A plain letter with its quiet a, as in sangat, takes the tippi. Same hum, different partner. There's a third mark in the family: the addhak, a small curve that tells you to double the next letter and lean on it. Now the part worth repeating tonight. The word Granth itself, in Gurmukhi, carries a tippi. Take it off, and the book's own name loses its n. Drop the tippi from sangat and you're left with sagat, which isn't the word at all: the gathering vanishes with one missing mark. So small marks matter isn't fussiness. Someone reading aloud in a gurdwara, or at a kitchen table for a grandparent, is carrying the sound to people who trust it. The marks are how a reader keeps that trust. They're tiny on the page and large in the ear.
screen: `BOTH ADD A HUM.` · `THE VOWEL SIGN PICKS THE MARK.` · `ADDHAK DOUBLES THE NEXT LETTER.` · `GRANTH NEEDS ITS TIPPI.` · then, large: `SMALL MARKS MATTER.`

segments.voice: Open a gutka, a steek or a Gurbani app to any page and hunt for one tippi or one bindi. When you find it, rest your eyes on it and say the word softly twice: once with the hum, once without, and hear what the small mark was holding up. Then breathe slowly, and let the hum fade on each breath out.
Tippi: a small curved mark above a Gurmukhi letter that adds a nasal hum, the n in sangat and in Granth. The fourth word of the year.
Keep this: small marks matter, and one of them can hold up a whole word. Four of twenty.

howItsDone: Learners of Gurmukhi are taught the tippi, the bindi and the addhak along with the vowel signs, and readers of Gurbani take care to sound the nasal marks so each word is heard as it is written.

notes: v3 puzzle day: why keep two nasal marks? Answer: they share a sound and split the work by vowel sign (the rule taught to learners today: bindi with kanna and the longer signs, tippi with a plain letter and some others).

The pairing rule is stated loosely on purpose ('in the rule learners are taught'); the Granth's own older orthography does not always follow modern Punjabi spelling. Confirm the examples ਸੰਗਤ (tippi), ਮਾਂ (bindi), ਗ੍ਰੰਥ (tippi) and that the simplification is fair.
Addhak described only as doubling the next letter; nothing is claimed about how often it appears in the Granth.
Gurmukhi ਟਿੱਪੀ, ਬਿੰਦੀ, ਅੱਧਕ, ਸੰਗਤ, ਗ੍ਰੰਥ and the sound-outs to be checked.
